sections.heading: Asking Jesus to fill me with his Spirit
sections.text: Lord Jesus Christ, fill me with your Spirit. Make me aware of his presence, not as an idea I mention, but as the living help I need right now. I am blind without him, so open my eyes. I am dark inside without your light, so let him speak light into me.
theological_themes: Dependence on Christ to give the Spirit
Spiritual blindness apart from God’s illumination
The Spirit’s personal presence and work in the believer

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that the Spirit guides believers into truth and glorifies Christ by taking what is Christ’s and making it known. This grounds the prayer for the Spirit to make Christ real and present to the believer.

Paul connects God’s original command for light to the inner illumination that reveals the glory of God in Christ. That directly supports the prayer’s cry for God to bring light into spiritual darkness.

sections.heading: Help me see what is already mine in you
sections.text: Give me faith to see what I so easily forget: that I am held by you, known by you, and not lost to you; that my whole self, body and soul, has been bought by your blood; and that my guilt is covered, not by anything I have done, but by your perfectly obedient life given for me.

scripture_references.connection: This passage states that redemption and forgiveness come through Christ’s blood according to God’s grace, supporting the prayer’s confidence that the believer belongs to Christ because he has paid the cost.

Paul contrasts Adam’s disobedience with Christ’s obedience, showing that Christ’s righteous obedience is counted for his people. This grounds the prayer’s trust that sin is covered by Christ’s life, not personal merit.

God speaks of his people as engraved on his hands, an image of permanent covenant remembrance. The prayer uses that kind of assurance to ask for faith to know that Christ will not forget or abandon his own.

sections.heading: Let me know how deeply I am joined to you
sections.text: Keep filling me with the Spirit’s revealing grace, so I truly understand that nothing can tear me away from you. Let me know that you have bound me to yourself forever—with righteousness, love, mercy, and faithfulness. Teach me to live as someone joined to you: like a branch living from the vine, like a house standing because its foundation is solid.
theological_themes: Christ as the source and foundation of the believer’s life

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes believers as branches that can bear fruit only by abiding in him, which fits the prayer’s image of life flowing from union with Christ.
God promises to betroth his people to himself in righteousness, steadfast love, mercy, and faithfulness. The prayer draws on this covenant language to express permanent belonging to Christ.
Paul says that Jesus Christ is the only foundation that can be laid. This supports the prayer’s image of the believer resting on Christ as a building rests on its foundation.

sections.heading: Make your Spirit my comfort, strength, and life
sections.text: Let your Spirit comfort me when I am sorrowful, strengthen me when I am under pressure, and renew me when I am tired. Make his presence in me bear real fruit: holiness that is not pretend, peace that holds, joy that lasts, prayer that keeps returning to you, and love for you that does not burn out.
theological_themes: Peace, joy, prayer, and devotion produced by the Spirit

scripture_references.connection: Paul prays that believers would abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit, linking the Spirit’s work with joy, peace, and sustaining confidence in God.
The fruit of the Spirit describes the kind of character and life the prayer asks God to produce—real holiness expressed in love, joy, peace, and other Spirit-formed virtues.
Paul says the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes when they do not know how to pray. This supports the request for the Spirit to keep prayer alive even in weariness and need.

sections.heading: Search me so I run to Christ, not myself
sections.text: Send your Spirit to search my heart. Show me more honestly where sin still twists me and how helpless I am apart from you. Do not let that knowledge drive me into despair or self-repair. Let it drive me to you—to run to you, hold on to you, and rest on you as the beginning, middle, and end of my salvation.
theological_themes: Christ as the whole source of salvation

scripture_references.connection: Jesus says the Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. This grounds the prayer for the Spirit to expose sin truthfully rather than leave the heart self-deceived.
The psalmist asks God to search him and reveal any grievous way in him so that God may lead him rightly. This parallels the prayer’s request for heart-searching that results in returning to God.
Jesus is described as the founder and perfecter of faith, which supports the prayer’s confession that salvation depends on Christ from start to finish.

sections.heading: Keep me from resisting the Spirit
sections.text: Please do not let me treat your Spirit with indifference, push him away through stubbornness, or give him a cold welcome while pretending to want you. Soften what is hard in me. Wake up what is sluggish. Bring me under your gracious rule. Lord, answer me for the honor of your great name.
theological_themes: Warning against grieving or resisting the Holy Spirit
Need for a softened and responsive heart
God’s glory as the ground of prayer

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, especially in the context of sinful patterns that contradict their new life. This supports the prayer’s concern not to respond to the Spirit with coldness or rebellion.

Stephen describes hard-hearted resistance to the Holy Spirit, showing that rebellion against God’s voice is a serious spiritual danger. The prayer turns that warning into a plea for mercy and softness.
God promises to replace a heart of stone with a heart of flesh and put his Spirit within his people. This supports the request for God to soften the heart and make obedience possible by the Spirit.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The prayer asks Jesus to send and fill the believer with the Spirit. This is broadly supported in Western Trinitarian theology and in New Testament passages where the risen Christ pours out or gives the Spirit, though the wording touches the historically contested East-West question of the Spirit’s procession.
The original uses strong language about human corruption and helplessness. I preserved that theological force without adding therapeutic categories or softening the doctrine of sin.

The marriage or betrothal imagery for the believer’s relationship to Christ is biblical but metaphorical; it should not be read in a sentimental or individualized way detached from its covenant context.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered “occupied with his presence” as being aware of the Spirit’s living help, because the original means more than thinking about the Spirit; it asks for the Spirit’s active, conscious presence to shape the whole inner life.

I interpreted “my name engraven in thy hand” through the biblical image of God’s permanent remembrance of his people, while keeping the prayer addressed to Christ because the original speaks directly to the Lord Jesus.

I rendered “my sinfulness covered by the life of pure obedience” as guilt covered by Christ’s obedient life given for me, preserving the Reformed emphasis on Christ’s active obedience without over-explaining it inside the prayer.

I changed “beginning and end of my salvation” to “beginning, middle, and end” to make the meaning explicit in contemporary language: Christ is not merely the initiator and finisher but the whole ground of salvation throughout.
